t.2.58.1: Having committed that great sin out of ignorance, my senses all confounded, I, alone, pondered in my mind: how might it now be set right?
t.2.58.2: Then, taking that pitcher filled with excellent water, I followed the path as it had been described to me and reached that hermitage.
t.2.58.3: There I saw his parents, weak, blind, aged and without anyone to guide them, like two birds whose wings have been clipped.
t.2.58.4: There I saw the two of them, seated and unable to move about, passing the time in talk about him, bereft of that hope because of me, listless and like those who have no protector.
t.2.58.5: Hearing the sound of my footsteps, the sage spoke these words: "Why do you delay, my son? Bring the water quickly."
t.2.58.6: Dear son, for what reason have you been playing in the water like this? This mother of yours is anxious; come quickly into the hermitage.
t.2.58.7: Whatever wrong was done to you, son, by your mother or by me, that should not be held in your mind, dear one, by you who are an ascetic.
t.2.58.8: You are the refuge of those who have no refuge, and you are the eye of those bereft of sight. Our lives are bound up in you, yet you do not speak a single word to us two.
t.2.58.9: Seeing that sage, I, frightened and as if stricken with fear, addressed him in an indistinct, faltering voice whose syllables were broken.
t.2.58.10: Steadying with great effort the working of my mind and the strength of my speech, I then told him of the dread born of the calamity that had befallen his son.
t.2.58.11: I am Daśaratha, a kṣatriya, not the son of the great-souled one. This sorrow, condemned by the virtuous and born of my own deed, has come upon me.
t.2.58.12: O blessed one, bow in hand, I came to the bank of the Sarayū, eager to kill some wild beast, or an elephant that had come to the watering place.
t.2.58.14: Then, going to the bank of the river, I saw an ascetic lying on the ground, his heart pierced by an arrow, his life departed.
t.2.58.15: O blessed one, having marked a sound in the water, I, wishing to kill an elephant, loosed an iron arrow, and by it your son has been slain.
t.2.58.13: There I heard the sound of a pitcher being filled in the water; thinking, "This is an elephant," I struck it with an arrow.
t.2.58.16: And when the arrow was drawn out, he went to heaven right there, grieving for his two revered parents and lamenting, "They are blind!"
t.2.58.17: Out of ignorance I struck down your son in haste. Now that things have come to this, may the sage be gracious to me in whatever remains to be done.
t.2.58.18: Having heard those harsh words, that man of great splendor, sighing and worn down by grief, spoke to me as I stood before him with joined palms.
t.2.58.19: If you had not yourself told me of this evil deed, O king, your head would at once have burst into a hundred thousand pieces.
t.2.58.20: O king, the slaying of a forest-dweller, above all, when done knowingly by a kṣatriya, would cast down from his place even the wielder of the thunderbolt.
t.2.58.21: Since this deed was done out of ignorance, for that very reason you still live; otherwise today the whole race of the Rāghavas would cease to be, so how much less would you survive?
t.2.58.22: "O king, lead the two of us to that place," he said to me. "Today we wish to see that son of ours, whom we shall behold for the last time."
t.2.58.23: I saw him, his limbs smeared with blood and his deerskin garment scattered, lying senseless on the ground, fallen into the power of Dharmarāja.
t.2.58.25: Approaching him and touching their own son, those two ascetics fell upon his body, and his father spoke these words.
t.2.58.24: Then I alone led those two, deeply stricken with grief, to that place, and made the sage, together with his wife, touch their son.
t.2.58.26: Am I not dear to you, son? Look at your mother, O righteous one! Why do you not embrace me, son? Speak a word, O tender one!
t.2.58.27: Or in the last part of the night, from whom shall I hear, as he recites, the sweet and heart-touching scripture, or especially anything else?
t.2.58.28: Who now, after bathing, worshipping at twilight and offering oblations into the fire, will sit beside me and cheer me, tormented as I am by grief and fear for my son?
t.2.58.29: Who now will gather bulbs, roots and fruits and feed me like a cherished guest, me who am helpless to act, without support and without a guide?
t.2.58.30: How, O son, shall I support this mother of yours, blind and aged, a poor ascetic woman, wretched and longing for her son?
t.2.58.32: And both of us, stricken with grief, helpless and wretched in the forest, bereft of you, shall very swiftly go to the abode of Yama.
t.2.58.31: Stay, son, do not, do not go to the abode of Yama! Tomorrow you shall go there with me, strengthened by your mother as well.
t.2.58.33: Then, on seeing Vaivasvata, I shall speak these words to him: 'May Dharmarāja be forgiving toward me; let this boy go on supporting his parents.'
t.2.58.34: As surely as you are sinless, my son, and were slain by one of sinful deeds, by the power of that truth go swiftly to the worlds that belong to those who fight with weapons.
t.2.58.35: O son, go to that supreme state which heroes attain who never turn back in battle and are slain while facing the foe.
t.2.58.36: The state that Sagara, Śaibya, Dilīpa, Janamejaya, Nahuṣa and Dhundhumāra attained, to that state go, my dear son.
t.2.58.38: Whatever state is attained by those who give away a thousand cows, whatever by those who serve their gurus, and whatever by those who lay down their bodies, go to that state, my dear son. For indeed, no one born in this family goes to an inauspicious end.
t.2.58.37: The destination that belongs to all the virtuous, the one that is won through Vedic study and through austerity, the destination of one who gives land, of one who has established the sacred fire, and of one who keeps the vow of a single wife.
t.2.58.39: Thus he lamented piteously there again and again; then, together with his wife, he set about offering the water libation for him.
t.2.58.40: But the sage's son, in a divine form gained through his own deeds, comforted his parents for a moment and then spoke these words.
t.2.58.41: Through serving you both I have attained a lofty place, and you two also shall soon come to my side.
t.2.58.42: Having spoken thus, the sage's son, master of his senses, swiftly ascended to heaven in a radiant, divine celestial chariot.
t.2.58.44: Slay me this very day, O king; I feel no anguish at death, since with your arrow you have made me, who had but one son, sonless.
t.2.58.43: Having quickly performed the water-offering together with his wife, that ascetic of great splendour spoke to me as I stood before him with joined palms.
t.2.58.45: Since my pure son has been slain by you through ignorance, I shall therefore lay upon you a curse, one of great sorrow and exceedingly dreadful.
t.2.58.46: Just as this sorrow born of calamity to my son is now mine, so too, O king, will you meet your death through grief for your son.
t.2.58.47: Therefore, good lady, the word of that noble one has now come upon me, that I shall today give up my life through grief for my son.
t.2.58.48: Even if Rāma were to touch me or embrace me just once today, still, O queen, what I have done to Rāghava was unworthy of me.
t.2.58.49: With my eyes I cannot see you, and my memory is slipping away. O Kausalyā, these messengers of Vaivasvata are hurrying me on.
t.2.58.50: What could be more sorrowful than this, that at the end of my life I do not see Rāma, the knower of dharma, whose valor is true?
t.2.58.51: Those who will see again, in the fifteenth year, the face of Rāma adorned with lovely, auspicious earrings are not men; they are gods.
t.2.58.52: Fortunate are those who will behold the face of Rāma, with eyes like lotus petals, fair brows, fine teeth and a lovely nose, a face like the lord of the stars.
t.2.58.53: Fortunate are those who will behold that fragrant face of my lord, which resembles the autumn moon and the full-blown lotus.
t.2.58.55: This grief, born of my own deeds, violently wears me down, helpless and senseless as I am, just as the current of a river wears away its bank.
t.2.58.54: Joyfully they will behold Rāma, his forest-dwelling ended, come back again to Ayodhyā, like Śukra returned to its proper course.
t.2.58.56: "Alas, Rāghava, mighty-armed one! Alas, you who dispelled my sorrows!" Lamenting thus, King Daśaratha reached the end of his life.
t.2.58.57: Thus speaking piteously, the lord of men, stricken by the exile of his beloved son, then, when midnight had passed, tormented by intense grief, gave up his life, he of noble appearance.
